text_blocks.snippet: Lung cancer staging is determined by assessing the extent of the cancer's spread, primarily using the TNM (Tumor, Node, Metastasis) system. This involves evaluating the tumor's size and location (T), involvement of nearby lymph nodes (N), and whether it has spread to distant organs (M). The results of various tests, including imaging scans (like CT, PET, and MRI), biopsies, and bronchoscopies, are used to determine these factors.
snippet_highlighted_words: by assessing the extent of the cancer's spread, primarily using the TNM (Tumor, Node, Metastasis) system

list.snippet: T (Tumor): Describes the size and location of the primary tumor within the lung.
N (Node): Indicates whether the cancer has spread to nearby lymph nodes and, if so, which ones.
M (Metastasis): Determines if the cancer has spread to distant organs or lymph nodes beyond the chest.

list.title: Imaging Scans:
list.snippet: CT scans, PET scans, and MRI scans are crucial for visualizing the tumor, assessing its size and location, and identifying any spread to lymph nodes or distant organs.

list.title: Biopsies:
list.snippet: Tissue samples are taken from the tumor and potentially lymph nodes to confirm the presence of cancer and determine its type (e.g., non-small cell lung cancer or small cell lung cancer).

list.title: Bronchoscopy:
list.snippet: A thin, flexible tube with a camera is inserted into the airways to visualize the tumor and collect tissue samples.

list.title: Other Tests:
list.snippet: Lung function tests may be performed to assess lung health, and blood tests may be used in some cases.
The results of these tests are combined to assign a stage to the cancer, using either a stage 1-4 system for non-small cell lung cancer or a limited/extensive system for small cell lung cancer.
The stage provides an estimate of the cancer's extent and helps doctors develop a treatment plan.
Staging is essential for determining the most appropriate treatment approach (e.g., surgery, chemotherapy, radiation therapy).
It also helps predict the potential outcome (prognosis) of the cancer.
Staging is also used to identify suitable clinical trials for patients.
